orders.trial_court_action: Denied Kaleida Health’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Dolinar alleged that she slipped in a puddle in a newly mopped hallway of a building owned and maintained by Kaleida Health.

legal_issues.finding: The plaintiff’s awareness of wetness did not extinguish the owner’s duty to keep the premises reasonably safe.
The owner failed to rule out negligent mopping that left enough water to form a puddle. Whether it created that condition remained triable.
The court identified actual notice as part of the movant’s burden and resolved the motion on the creation issue.
Constructive notice was part of the initial standard. The court did not make a separate factual finding on it.
The court rejected the argument that an observable wet floor and Dolinar’s awareness required dismissal.
The court treated the visibility and awareness argument as bearing only on comparative negligence, without apportioning fault.

quality.notes: Ownership and maintenance are express. The opinion does not identify the building’s specific use or the plaintiff’s role.

evidence.quote: Kristina Dolinar, Respondent, v Kaleida Health, Appellant.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Erie County (J. David Sampson, A.J.), entered August 19, 2016. The order denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing plaintiff's complaint.
It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.

Plaintiff commenced this action seeking to recover damages for injuries she sustained when she allegedly slipped and fell in a puddle in a hallway that had just been mopped in a building owned and maintained by defendant.
We conclude that Supreme Court properly denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Defendant had the initial burden on the motion of establishing that it did not create the allegedly dangerous condition and that it did not have actual or constructive notice thereof

We agree with the court, specifically, that defendant failed to establish that it did not create the allegedly dangerous condition by negligently mopping the area and leaving excess water on the floor sufficient to create a puddle, and thus there is an issue of fact with respect thereto
We reject defendant's contention that the court should have granted the motion because the wet condition of the floor was readily observable and plaintiff was aware that the floor was wet.
That contention concerns only "the issue of plaintiff's comparative negligence" and does "not negate defendant's duty to keep the premises reasonably safe"
and thus it does not establish defendant's entitlement to judgment as a matter of law.

orders.description: New York County order entered October 31, 2018
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motions dismissing the complaint and denied Glueck’s cross-motion for summary judgment on liability.

facts.factual_summary: Glueck alleged that she tripped while exiting defendants’ premises, where there were two exterior steps. She offered different accounts, including that she missed a step. Neither she nor the nonparty witnesses could identify the exact fall site.

legal_issues.finding: Glueck could not identify the cause or location, the witnesses had not seen her fall, and photographs showed steps in good repair without a visible defect or foreign substance.
The engineer alleged building-code violations. The court rejected the report without finding a violation.
The engineering report was unsworn, speculative and conclusory.
The unsworn report was inadmissible on summary judgment, and the court upheld denial of Glueck’s cross-motion.

evidence_discussed.description: The record recounted Glueck’s differing versions, including a missed step.
Nonparty witnesses assumed where she fell but had not observed the fall.
Photographs depicted two steps in good repair, without broken surfaces or foreign substances.
Glueck relied on an engineer’s code opinion. The court rejected it on form and substance.

quality.notes: The claimed route was out of defendants’ premises, but the court explicitly found the fall location unidentified. Private control of the actual fall site remains unresolved. The affirmance and alleged trip are clear.

evidence.quote: Grace Glueck, Appellant, v Starbucks Corporation et al., Respondents.

Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Robert R. Reed, J.), entered October 31, 2018, which granted defendants' motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, and denied plaintiff's cross motion for summary judgment on the issue of liability, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
Defendants' motions for summary judgment were properly granted
plaintiff alleges that she was injured when she tripped and fell while exiting defendants' premises; the entrance/exit to the premises has two steps outside the building.

The record shows that plaintiff, who was walking with a cane, could not identify the cause or location of her fall, giving multiple versions of the accident, including stating that she had missed a step
Nor could the nonparty witnesses identify the location of plaintiff's accident, stating that they made assumptions as to where plaintiff may have fallen, but did not actually see her fall.

Plaintiff was unable to identify any defective condition at the location of her fall, the photographs of the area in front of the premises depicted two steps, in good repair, and there were no cracked or broken surfaces or foreign substances.

Plaintiff's reliance on the report of an engineering expert, who opined that there were violations of New York City Building Codes of 1916 and 1938 and unspecified recent codes that incorporate a certain standard of the American National Standards Institute
The report is unsworn and is therefore inadmissible for the purposes of summary judgment
In any event, the report is speculative and conclusory
In view of the foregoing, plaintiff's cross motion for summary judgment on the issue liability was properly denied.

orders.description: Bronx County order entered on or about June 6, 2014
orders.trial_court_action: Granted the building owner’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Brooks-Torrence alleged that she slipped on urine dripping from the stairwell handrails. She did not see urine on the step beforehand but saw a puddle when she returned about 20 minutes later.

legal_issues.finding: The owner made a prima facie showing that it did not create the urine condition, and plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue.
The guard recalled no complaint about the staircase that day before the fall. The court found the owner had shown lack of actual notice.
The plaintiff’s testimony did not establish how long the urine had been present. It could have been deposited moments before the fall.

evidence_discussed.description: Brooks-Torrence described what she saw before the fall and on returning.
The security guard testified that she did not recall a pre-accident complaint.

quality.notes: The source describes ownership but does not identify the building’s use or the injured person’s relationship to it.

evidence.quote: Rhonda Brooks-Torrence, Appellant, v Twin Parks Southwest, Respondent.

Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Mark Friedlander, J.), entered on or about June 6, 2014, which granted defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
Plaintiff alleges that she was descending a staircase in a building owned by defendant when she slipped and fell on urine that was dripping off of the stairwell's handrails.

Plaintiff testified that she did not see urine on the step before she fell, but that she saw a puddle of urine on the landing area and the step after she returned to the accident location about 20 minutes after the accident.
Defendant made a prima facie showing that it neither created the urine condition, nor had actual or constructive notice of its existence

by submitting the deposition testimony of a security guard who was stationed at the building at the time of the accident; she testified that she did not recall receiving a complaint about the staircase on the day of the accident before the incident occurred.

Defendant showed that it lacked constructive notice of the urine on the staircase, by submitting plaintiff's deposition testimony, which shows that the urine that caused her to fall "could have been deposited there only minutes or seconds before the accident[,] and any other conclusion would be pure speculation"
In opposition, plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.

orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: After buying yogurt at a Staten Island McDonald’s, Rivero allegedly slipped on a damp floor that an employee had recently mopped. A wet-floor sign stood in the area of the fall.

legal_issues.finding: The restaurant satisfied its duty to warn by placing a warning sign in the area of the fall. The plaintiff raised no triable issue in opposition.
The court could not hold as a matter of law that the damp floor was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous. Dismissal rested on the warning actually given.

evidence_discussed.description: The opinion identifies a wet-floor sign in the accident area without specifying how its placement was proved.

quality.notes: P001 uses “defendant” once while describing the walk to the table. The surrounding account and P002 expressly identify the plaintiff as the person who slipped.

evidence.quote: the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Richmond County (McMahon, J.), dated June 30, 2011, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.
At approximately 9:40 p.m. on May 5, 2009, the plaintiff allegedly was injured at a McDonald’s Restaurant on Staten Island owned by the defendant.
Specifically, the plaintiff had purchased a yogurt at the counter and asked the counter worker where the restroom was located.
he slipped and fell on a damp floor which had been mopped by an employee shortly before the occurrence.
At the time of the occurrence, a wet floor sign was in place in the area where the plaintiff fell.
A property owner has a duty to maintain its property in a reasonably safe condition, which “may also include the duty to warn of a dangerous condition”

On this record, it cannot be determined as a matter of law that the damp floor upon which the plaintiff slipped and fell was open and obvious, and not inherently dangerous, so as to relieve the defendant of its duty to warn of the hazard

However, the defendant established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that it satisfied its duty to warn of a potentially dangerous condition by placing a warning sign in the area where the plaintiff fell
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact

orders.trial_court_action: Denied Melamed’s motion to vacate the March 2019 default order and obtain denial of defendants’ summary judgment motion.

facts.factual_summary: Melamed alleged that she tripped and fell inside premises owned by defendants on October 20, 2014. The opinion specifies no hazard or more precise location.

legal_issues.finding: Counsel’s calendaring explanation did not establish a reasonable excuse for the default. The court therefore did not reach whether Melamed had a potentially meritorious opposition.

evidence_discussed.description: Counsel’s affirmation attributed the default to a motion clerk’s calendaring error and an anticipated adjournment. The court deemed the explanation conclusory and unsubstantiated.

quality.notes: Only the June 2020 order refusing to vacate the default was before the court. The March 2019 dismissal is procedural history; the appeal did not decide the negligence merits.

evidence.quote: Nataliya Melamed, Appellant, v Adams & Company Real Estate, LLC, et al., Respondents.

the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Edgar G. Walker, J.), dated June 24, 2020. The order denied the plaintiff's motion pursuant to CPLR 5015 (a) (1) to vacate so much of an order of the same court dated March 15, 2019, as granted that branch of the defendants' unopposed motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, and thereupon to deny that branch of the defendants' motion.
Ordered that the order dated June 24, 2020, is affirmed, with costs.
On October 20, 2014, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell inside of premises owned by the defendants.

An attorney employed by the law firm representing the plaintiff appeared in court on the agreed-upon March 15, 2019 return date, but no opposition to the defendants' motion was filed. In an order dated March 15, 2019, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted that branch of the defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the plaintiff's default in opposing the motion.
In an order dated June 24, 2020, the Supreme Court denied the plaintiff's motion. The plaintiff appeals.

A party seeking to vacate an order entered upon his or her default in opposing a motion must demonstrate both a reasonable excuse for the default and a potentially meritorious opposition to the motion

Here, in support of her motion, the plaintiff submitted an affirmation of an attorney employed by the law firm representing her who stated that a "motion clerk" employed by the firm had improperly calendared the defendants' motion in the firm's computer system as being "on for the first time" on March 15, 2019, and that, as a result, "the attorney assigned to oppose [the d]efendants' motion assumed an adjournment would be granted in Court on the return date of March 15, 2019."

This explanation is conclusory and unsubstantiated, and, under the circumstances presented here, insufficient to demonstrate a reasonable excuse for the plaintiff's default in opposing the defendants' motion, inter alia, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint

Since the plaintiff failed to demonstrate a reasonable excuse for her default, it is unnecessary to determine whether she demonstrated the existence of a potentially meritorious opposition to the defendants' motion

Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the plaintiff's motion pursuant to CPLR 5015 (a) (1) to vacate so much of the order dated March 15, 2019, as granted that branch of the defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, and thereupon to deny that branch of the defendants' motion.
